image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Top:** Horizontal **stacked bar chart** showing cost components of an imported sneaker.
- **Bottom:** **Treemap** showing number/share of shoes imported in 2023 by country.

## 2) Layout techniques
- The visualization combines **two different chart panels** stacked vertically.
- **Top panel:** uses **stacking** within a single horizontal bar.
- **Bottom panel:** uses **area-based subdivision** (treemap / rectangular tiling), not faceting.
- No small multiples or repeated facets are visible.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Cost component category (Materials and labor, Manufacturer margin, Shipping and logistics, Tariff) | Categorical/nominal | Segment position within stacked bar, segment length/width, color/hue, text labels |
| Import cost total ($26) | Quantitative | Text annotation/label |
| Country (China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Treemap rectangle grouping, text labels, color/hue |
| Share/number of shoes imported in 2023 (shown as percentages: 59%, 23%, 6%, 11%) | Quantitative | Rectangle area in treemap, percentage labels |
| Year (2023) | Temporal | Title/annotation |

comments.raw_comment:
Three countries in Asia make and send all but 11% of US shoes across the Pacific on ships to arrive at coastal ports.  (They don’t arrive in San Diego, because the Port of San Diego, which is in National City east of San Diego and west of Chula Vista, imports vehicles — too small to compete with Long Beach.)
    
    So all these shoes make their way from there to here and now a new tariff will add $5 on top of $21 on average to the cost every pair.  
    
    Will people who like spiffy, fun shoes be willing to pay that extra five bucks?  Will it be just $5 extra, or will trucking fees, storage fees, and salesperson pay and storefront rental be layered on top as percent markup?
    
    What do shoes really truly cost to make and get into the hands of the person who puts them on their feet?
    
    Who are the other 11%?
    
    Is any shoe we wear made here?
    
    Do we really need all those shiny new vehicles from Asia that come into the Port of San Diego?  Or will GHG be less impacted if we hang onto older, but efficient, cars for longer, each of us?
    
    Or maybe walk in those shoes a little further?
